utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everybody. Madam Registrar, could you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-83-T, the Prosecutor versus Rasim Delic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could we have appearances for the day, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours, Counsel, and everyone in and around the courtroom. Daryl Mundis for the Prosecution. I'm assisted today by my case managers Alma Imamovic and Fraser McIlwraith.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. For the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to my learned friends. Good afternoon to everyone. Vasvija Vidovic and Nicholas Robson on behalf of General Delic. Our case manager is Lejla Gluhic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Vidovic. Good afternoon, sir. Will you please stand up.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Will you please make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may be seated. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, for the record, can you please state your full name?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: Velibor Trivicevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, Mr. Trivicevic, can you please state your date of birth and place of birth?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: 25th of April, 1970, Prnjavor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Trivicevic, can you please tell the Trial Chamber how you were employed when the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina began?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: At the beginning of the war, I was doing my regular military term, the former JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And when did your term of service in the JNA come to an end?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: My term of service came to an end the 17th of January, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Trivicevic, following the 17th of January, 1992, were you gainfully employed, and if so, in what capacity?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: I started working at the Prnjavor Health Centre as a paramedic. I was working with the ambulance.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did there come a time, sir, after the 17th of January, 1992, when you joined a military force, and if so, which military force did you join?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: I had been called up by the Prnjavor sector of the Defence Ministry, and I joined the Army of the Republika Srpska on the 28th [Realtime transcript read in error "20th"] of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, what unit of the Army of the Republika Srpska did you join?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: It was the 1st Light Infantry Brigade in Prnjavor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: How long, sir, did you continue serving in the VRS 1st Light Infantry Brigade of Prnjavor?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: I continued serving in the Brigade until the 1st of January, 1993, when I left the unit and again joined the 1st Light Infantry Brigade on the 4th of August, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: When you rejoined that unit on the 4th of August, 1994, Mr. Trivicevic, what were your military duties or responsibilities?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: My duties, in purely civilian terms, was to work as a paramedic with the medical unit of the 1st Light Infantry Brigade. I was attached to the medical unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: In July 1995, Mr. Trivicevic, can you please tell us where you were deployed?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: It was at a position held by the 3rd Battalion of our unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, where was this position held by the 3rd Battalion of the 1st Light Infantry Brigade?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: It was near the Krcevine hamlet, Lozna village, Banovici municipality, in the Ozren theatre of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I'll return to that in just a moment, sir, but I believe there might be an error in the transcript. It indicates on line 8 of page 3 that you joined the VRS on the 20th of June, 1992. Is that, in fact, the correct date, 20 June 1992?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: The 28th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Mr. Trivicevic, at the time the 3rd Battalion of the 1st Light Infantry Brigade of the VRS was near the Krcevine hamlet, what armed force or unit was on the other side of the front line?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: According to our information at the time, facing us on the other side of the front was the BH Army, led by the El Mujahedin Detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you specifically tell the Trial Chamber, sir, the location where you personally were in the month of July 1995?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: At the time I was captured, I was at Radovan Todorovic's house in Krcevine hamlet, about 300 metres behind the front line. I believe that was the name of the man that the house belonged to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, Mr. Trivicevic, what were you doing in Radovan Todorovic's house in Krcevine hamlet in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: There had been an action by the Mujahedin on the 27th of May, 1995. Our part of the unit was cut off as a result of this action, and the wounded couldn't be helped in a timely manner, so we were forced to set up a forward medical post in order to help those people, the wounded. I was working as a paramedic at this forward post.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And at this forward medical post in Radovan Todorovic's house in Krcevine in July 1995, were you the only person with medical training at that forward medical post?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just before the witness answers, can I just check something? The previous answer said the witness said: "There had been an action by the Mujahedin on the 27th of May, 1995." The next question said: "Now, at this forward medical post in Radovan Todorovic's house in July 1995." Is it May or July?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: We can ask the witness to again clarify that, but I believe he said as a result of the 27th of May, 1995, his unit was cut off, and as a result they established the forward medical post.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Is that clear from the record, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I accept your explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Trivicevic, let me return, then, to the forward medical post in Radovan Todorovic's house in Krcevine. During the month of July 1995, other than yourself, were there any persons at that medical post with medical training or experience?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: There were just three of us at the house, the doctor, Branko Sikanic, a medical student, second-year student, Miroslav Knezevic, and I.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Trivicevic, you told us a few moments ago that you were captured. Can you tell the Trial Chamber the date that you were captured?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: On the 21st of July, 1995. It was a Friday, as a matter of fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you please briefly tell the Trial Chamber what you recall happening on 21 July 1995, beginning from the time you woke up on that day?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: We were awoken by sounds of shooting on that day, small arms firing and shells going off. We, the medical unit, got ourselves ready. We went down to the cellar of that house in which we were staying in order to be ready to take in any wounded, and it was obvious that there would be wounded people. Soon the first wounded started coming in, and we tried to help them. We gave them first aid. After that, I came out of the cellar, stepped out in front of the house, and I saw the column of people moving from the front line and in the direction of our house. I assumed that those were people from our side of the front line, our end of the front line, trying to retreat in an organised manner, so I told Branko Sikanic, the doctor, that we should go back to our rooms, get our equipment, get the wounded, and that those people would help us get the wounded out of the area. We went back into the house. However, as soon as we were back out, we dashed out of the house and straight into a group of Mujahedin standing there. Actually, we were right in front of them when we stepped out of the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you at this point, sir, and ask a couple of follow-up questions. You told us, as reflected on page 6, line 9: "We were awoken by sounds of shooting on that day." Do you recall, Mr. Trivicevic, approximately what time the shooting began on 21 July 1995?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember the exact time, but I think it was --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the witness please repeat the time? The interpreter didn't understand the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, you've been asked by the interpreter to repeat the time, because the interpreters didn't understand what you said.

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: It could have been quarter to or 10 to 4.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Trivicevic, you also told us, as reflected on page 6, line 23: "We dashed out of the house and straight into a group of Mujahedin standing there." My first question, sir, is: When you say,"We dashed out of the house," whom are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: I was referring to myself and Dr. Sikanic, because we were the only people who went back to the house to get the stuff that was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, when you say you ran straight into a group of Mujahedin standing there, can you tell us about this group of Mujahedin, in terms of how many, what they were wearing, what type of weapons, if any, they were carrying, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: At the time, they were standing some 30 metres away from me. I realised that they were a group of about ten. I don't know exactly how many there were, though. There were two or three men standing there who were talking in a language that we understood, that was intelligible to us. They were carrying automatic rifles, and for the most part they were carrying sabres, axes, and other such sharp implements.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, I'm not sure if the record -- or the transcript accurately reflected what you said. The language that they were speaking, could you understand that language or not?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: This was a group of ten, and there were two or three in that group who spoke in a language that we understood. The remaining part were using a language that we did not understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: This group of approximately ten people, what type of clothing were they wearing?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: They weren't all wearing the same type of uniform. They even were wearing some civilian clothes, bits and pieces of civilian clothing items, in a manner of speaking, different types of uniforms. Those weren't standard-issue military uniforms. They were wearing all sorts of different military uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall, sir, seeing any type of insignia on any of the items of military uniforms that were worn by these people?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't remember any of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, you told us a few moments ago, as reflected on line 23 of page 7, that they were standing "some 30 metres away from me." Can you tell us what happened after you saw them standing some 30 metres away?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: I came running out of that room in which we were helping the wounded. However, there was no one outside that room. They probably noticed that a Mujahedin unit had arrived, and they left the place. The Mujahedin started shouting in an unintelligible language, shouting for us to surrender. I realised that there was no way out for me, that I had no choice but to surrender, so I put my hands up in the air, which was a token of surrender.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I just ask one little question. I know I should have asked it a little earlier. Sir, at page 7, lines 17 to 18, in response to a question to who you were referring when you said, "We dashed out of the house," you said that it was yourself and Dr. Sikanic. Can I just ask, what became of Miroslav Knezevic? Was he not with you at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Miroslav Knezevic stayed back with the wounded in the room in which we were helping them. When we went back into the house, there were all the people that were being helped, who were being treated, and all those taking care of them, and then they all left the place. He's still listed as missing to this very day. Some of the people who left the house on that day are still alive and well, fortunately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may proceed, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, sir, you told us that you placed your hands above your head, up in the air, "I put my hands up in the air, which was a token of surrender." What happened after you put your hands up in the air?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: Well, in the meantime Dr. Sikanic came running out of the house. He realised what was going on, too. He ran straight to the cellar, probably to conceal our lists and everything else that he was keeping at the time. Their interpretation of this, however, was that he was commencing combat, and that's why they opened fire. The firing went on for some time before the doctor decided to surrender, and he came out of the house together with me, and they were shouting, "Surrender, surrender." I said, "What else should I do, put my hands up in the air?" For me, that was tantamount to surrender. There were Bosnians in that group, and they started saying that in the Arab world, in order to surrender, one lies down on the ground and places one's hands at the nape of one's neck, which as a result of that instruction, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me again, sir, interrupt you and ask a couple of follow-up questions. You told us: "They were shouting, 'Surrender, surrender.'" Do you recall, sir, who was shouting, "Surrender, surrender," to you?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: The handful of men from that group were shouting something in a language that we didn't understand. However, there were two or three men in that group who spoke in Serbian, and those were telling us that what the other men were shouting, "Men, surrender, surrender." They repeated this a couple of times, suggesting that we should surrender as ordered by those other men.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: At this point in time, sir, when you lay down and put your hands at the nape of your neck, do you know where Miroslav Knezevic and the wounded men were?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: At this point in time, I did not see any of these people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And just so that the record is clear, Mr. Trivicevic, where was Dr. Sikanic at the time you lay down and placed your hands at the nape of your neck?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: We did that together. Just moments before he had raised his arms, he had come out of the cellar, and he was now standing next to me, which means that we both lay down on the ground together.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Trivicevic, as members of the medical profession serving in the VRS, what distinctive insignia, if any, did you wear on your uniforms indicating that you were members of the medical profession?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: None. There was a red cross that we drew on a wall of the house, which meant there was a medical station in the house, but we wore no insignia at all distinguishing us from anybody else as members of a medical unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Trivicevic, are you in a position to indicate or to approximate the time of day on 21 July 1995 that you and Dr. Sikanic surrendered to this group of ten Mujahedin?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: This was sometime at daybreak, quarter past 4.00, half past 4.00 in the morning, but I can't be more accurate than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you describe for the Trial Chamber, to the best of your recollection, the weather conditions, including visibility, at the time you surrendered on 21 July 1995?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: It was a clear day. Visibility, 50/50, you could say. This was daybreak, so as far as visibility was concerned, this was a point in the day that was neither day nor night, in a manner of speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: After you and Dr. Sikanic surrendered on 21 July 1995, did the persons to whom you surrendered take you somewhere, take you and Dr. Sikanic somewhere?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: There were several places at which we stopped provisionally, but then eventually they took us to the village of Livade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Trivicevic, in a few moments I'm going to ask you about the village of Livade, but you've told us that you stopped at several places, you stopped provisionally. Can you just, at this point in time, tell the Trial Chamber the locations where you stopped while being taken to Livade?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: We first stopped outside the house where the Battalion Command used to be and then outside a trench on our end of the line, and then near the medical unit on the other side, the Mujahedin medical unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, when you say "the house where the Battalion Command used to be," do you know or can you tell us which battalion you're referring to when you say "the house where the Battalion Command used to be"?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: The Command of the 3rd Battalion of the 1st Light Infantry Brigade of Prnjavor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And that's the VRS unit that you belonged to; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you briefly tell the Trial Chamber what, if anything, happened while you were at this house while being escorted to Livade by the ten Mujahedin?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: We were being escorted by three of the Mujahedin. The others had already left. They took us outside the house and threw us down on the ground. They used a pair of scissors that they had previously found among our medical tools, and they shore my hair off, saying they were doing this to distinguish a dog from one of their brethren. They took all of the stuff that we were wearing off us, the silver chain that I was wearing, the money, German marks, the dinars. They seized everything, my driving license, my military identification booklet, because there were photographs inside. They wanted to show me how I would end up burning in hell because I stood up against Allah [Realtime transcript read in error "a law"]. One of the Bosnians in that group walked back to where we were standing. He had a wound to his lower leg. I asked to help him, to dress his wound, and they said I wouldn't be allowed to help one of their brothers. And he just put a bandage around his leg saying, "Allah has been merciful on me," and he just walked on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is that -- just a clarification. You said they said, "You're going to burn because you stood up against ..."?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were burning my documents, my driving license, my military identification booklet, because my photographs were inside. Those, they set fire to those to show us how we would end up burning in hell because we stood up to or against Allah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may proceed, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Trivicevic, you told us at line 2 of page 13: "They shore my hair off, saying that they were doing this to distinguish a dog from one of their brethren." What did that mean to you?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: Since I had the same sort of beard that I -- then that I have now, and all the Mujahedin wear a beard, I needed to look different from them. That's how I understood that at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, you also told us, sir, that one of the, as you put it, provisional stops was at a trench. Can you tell us -- you said "outside a trench on our end of the line." This is line 12 of page 12. Can you describe or tell us what happened at this trench on "our end of the line," as you put it?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: When they brought us to the pine woods near a trench and a dugout, there was a body in front with its head cut off.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you see anything next to this body with the head cut off?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was a large axe next to the body.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you know whose body that was that you saw near this trench?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know whose body it was, although they were showing documents belonging to Bogomir Danicic. However, that day, that man had escaped. He saved himself, leaving his documents behind. I thought that that was that man until I was released, but actually it turned out that he was alive. So I don't know who the dead body belonged to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: While you were at this location near the trench, sir, did anything else occur or happen while you were there?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: Next to the body with the cut-off head, they knocked me down first to the ground, and then also they did the same thing to Igor Sikanic [as interpreted]. One of the Mujahedin who was escorting us took the axe, shouting, "Allah Ekber." He struck the axe into the ground immediately next to my head.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Again, sir, on line 25, continuing on to line 1 of page 15, it indicates "they did the same thing to Igor Sikanic." Is that correctly reflected in the transcript?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: No. Igor is not "Sikanic." The first name of Sikanic is "Branko." It's "Dr. Sikanic."

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, finally, sir, you told us again, and this is reflected on lines 11 through 13 of page 12, that you made a provisional stop near the medical unit on the other side, the Mujahedin medical unit. Can you tell the Trial Chamber what, if anything, happened when you made a stop at that location?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: We stayed for a long time at that place. All kinds of things happened there. I don't know specifically what you are thinking of so that I can respond precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: How were you treated while you were temporarily at this location?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: First, they brought us, and then the doctor came from the medical unit who was wearing green surgical scrubs. He had a stethoscope, and when we said that we were colleagues, the doctor came out and he slapped us in front of everybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And who was this doctor that you're referring to wearing the green surgical scrubs?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I think that that was the doctor from the El Mudjahedin Detachment. I never saw that man again later, so I don't know exactly who it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And after this incident where you were slapped, did anything else happen?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: Then they knocked us all down onto a pile of gravel. They tied our hands and -- legs and hands to our back, and then somebody who was there from the medical unit brought out a medical knife, and in front of us he wrote on a piece of paper, "This is the end of Chetniks," and then he stuck that piece of paper onto the small knife.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And just so that we're clear, Mr. Trivicevic, when you say,"They knocked us all down," who are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: Us. Every time I say "us," it refers to myself and to Dr. Sikanic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, this piece of paper that said, "This is the end of the Chetniks," did it remain on the small knife?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: Having seen that they did not achieve the effect that they wanted to of frightening us with that small knife, later they brought a large knife and stuck it into the sand, and then stuck the piece of paper on that. Later, when we were transported in the car, they stuck that same piece of paper onto Dr. Sikanic's back, and he arrived at Livade with that same piece of paper stuck to his back.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let's turn now, sir, to your arrival in Livade. Do you recall approximately what time you arrived in that village on that day?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know the exact time. In my estimate, it could have been around 7.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: In the morning or in the evening?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: In the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And what was the date?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: The 21st of July, the same day that we were captured.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: In which year, sir, just for the record?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And when you arrived in Livade, can you tell the Trial Chamber where you were taken to in that village?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: We were placed into a warehouse where there were many boxes and tins of food.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And just for the record, sir, how long did you eventually remain in this warehouse in Livade?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: We stayed there until noon that same day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you see -- other than Dr. Sikanic, did you see any other people in this warehouse?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: In that warehouse, there was a group. I don't know the exact number. It was about 10 or 11 people. I'd forgotten the number, Muslims, who were on our side, who were captured by the Mujahedin during an action. But since they didn't know exactly who they were, they brought them there just in case so they could just check them out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you know any of these 10 or 11 Muslims that you saw in this house -- in this warehouse in Livade?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: I knew one of them very well. As for the rest, I knew them by sight, from seeing them around the town of Prnjavor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you remember the name of the one that you knew very well?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: His last name was Djodjic. I forgot his first name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And when you say, sir, "These Muslims were on our side," what were they doing on your side, if you know?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: These were people who had refused the summons to join the Army of Republika Srpska, and they were mobilised by going to the lines, to dig trenches, to bring food, so they were doing some auxiliary tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You told us, sir, as reflected on line 12 of page 17, that you remained in the warehouse until noon. What happened or where were you taken at noon on 21 July 1995?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: Just one moment. Before that, I just want to emphasise that in the meantime, maybe an hour after we got there, Igor Guljevatej was brought to the warehouse. He was our soldier on our line. So from that point in time on, there were three of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And let me just -- let me just ask you at this point, sir: Do you know what unit Igor Guljevatej was in?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He was in our units. He was a fighter in the 3rd Battalion of the Light Infantry Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, now can you tell us where Dr. Sikanic, Igor Guljevatej and yourself were taken around noon on 21 July 1995?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: At around noon, they transferred us to a nearby house. It was an older house that was a house on two floors, or the ground floor -- it had a ground floor and a first floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And for how long in total, sir, did you remain with the other two men in that house?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: We stayed in that house until the morning of the 23rd of July, until Sunday, in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber what happened to you while you were in that house from noon on the 21st of July until the morning of 23 July 1995?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: I can tell you everything that happened. First, the man came who actually brought us there. He removed shoes and socks from all of us, so all we wore were trousers and a T-shirt. Then first I was taken into a room where, before that, the Muslims who had been captured were taken. In front of them, he knocked me down to the floor. He took a sabre or a sword. He sat on my back, and he lifted my head in order to explain to them how Serbs and Chetniks should be treated, to demonstrate how to cut their throat.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me, sir, stop you at this point in time, briefly. You just mentioned that the Muslims who had been captured were in this room. Were these the same 10 or 11 Muslims that you'd seen earlier in the warehouse or were they different Muslims?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: No, they were the same people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you please continue describing what happened?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: Then he took my T-shirt and rolled it back over my head, and he placed a rope and tied it over the T-shirt, around my neck. Then he tightened the binding on my arms on my back. Then he bent my legs to the back and tied them to the hands. And then after that, he again tied my hands on my back. He did the same thing with the other two. He came several times to touch our hands, and for as long as they were soft, he went away. But when the hands hardened because of the swelling, he came, he untied us. He placed us in a corner of the room opposite from the place where the people who were in the room were sitting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, do you know what, if anything, happened to Dr. Sikanic or Igor Guljevatej while they were with you in this house in Livade?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: The same thing was repeated. The same thing that was done to me was done to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you receive, sir, any food while you were detained in this house?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. At one point, the Mujahedin came, and they brought food for the Muslims. They asked them if they received anything to eat while they were with us, and when they answered affirmatively, they gave us also some fish and a can of food.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did anything happen while you were eating the fish?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us, sir, what else happened or what else you observed while you were in this house in Livade?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: After what happened, you could hear shouting and noise in front of the house. I didn't know what was happening, with shouts "Allahu Ekber." One of the Mujahedin who was guarding us ran out of the room, and very quickly he came back to the room where we were, carrying in his arms the cut-off head of a person who I knew before. His name was Momir Mitrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us, Mr. Trivicevic, whether Momir Mitrovic during the war was a civilian or a soldier?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: Momir Mitrovic was a soldier in the 1st Battalion of the 1st Infantry Brigade of Prnjavor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us, sir, what happened when this person brought Momir Mitrovic's head into the room?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: He entered carrying the head in both of his hands in front of him. He was holding the head in front of us and asked if we knew that man. I obviously knew him from before, but I didn't dare say that. I said that I didn't know him, and the other two repeated the same thing. He placed the hand [as interpreted] in a fruit cardboard box and took it outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, excuse me for interrupting, sir, but the record again, I believe, has an error. It indicates on line 8 of page 21: "He placed the hand in a fruit cardboard box." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: He placed the head of Momir Mitrovic into a cardboard box and took it out of the room.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What happened after the head of Momir Mitrovic was taken out of the room in a cardboard box?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: The same man returned to the room carrying a different head that had fresh blood pouring from it, and again he held it in front of us and asked us if we knew the person. I didn't know that man, but I recollect every single feature on his face. And later, when I was freed, a woman, that man's sister, was carrying photographs around, asking if I knew anything about that man. And in those photographs, I recognised the man whose head had been cut off. That was Predrag Knezevic. He was also a member of the 1st Battalion of the Prnjavor 1st Light Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What happened to the head of Predrag Knezevic?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: The procedure was repeated. He placed that head also into a box and carried it out of the house. I don't really know what happened after that with the bodies and the heads.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Trivicevic, after this scene where these two heads were brought into the room, what happened to you and the other two men, Dr. Sikanic and Igor Guljevatej?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: We stayed there for a while, and then some people came who settled into the room next-door. The Muslims who were there took us by impaling our tied limbs on a stick, and that's how they carried us off for interrogation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You just told us, sir, that your tied -- "our tied limbs on a stick." How long did you remain with your limbs tied on a stick?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: There were two ways of tying us up. One of them was when we had bindings around our neck and our head was thrown back and our arms and legs were tied around the back. The other way was to have a pole inserted behind our knees, and then our head would be bent forward. So it depended. Over those two days, they would change the way they tied us. When they got tired of tying us in one way, they would tie us in another way. It wasn't specific. Later, they untied us, and however they tied us, that's how we remained throughout that first night. I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And can you explain to us, sir, when you say: "The other way was to have a pole inserted behind our knees and then our head would be bent forward," what would they do with your head when you were in that position with the stick beneath or behind your knees?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: Nothing. They would simply slip the rope around our neck, and then they would tighten that towards our knees, and we would remain tied to this pole the whole night. And then they would alternate periodically the way in which they tied us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Other than these means of tying you, sir, were you in any other way or were you or the other two men mistreated in any way?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: Occasionally, they would let the civilians from the village into the house, meaning young men, even elderly grandmothers came to look at the Chetniks. They even allowed them to take the poles that they used to tie us up with to beat us with.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, while you were at this house in Livade, were there guards guarding you and the other two men?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: We were never left alone in the room. There would always be someone of the Mujahedin with a rifle at the ready.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And did the people who guard you speak your language or a different language?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: They did not speak our language.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Trivicevic, you mentioned a few moments ago that you were taken while tied on this pole to be interrogated. Can you describe or tell us about this interrogation?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: Two men from the room who were with us picked us up on those poles and carried us to this other room, where there were two men. I remember one of them very well. I saw that man later at the Zenica detention facility. The other one, all I recall of him is that he had a moustache. So I really remember him sitting down and talking to me, but I really don't know who he was or if I would recognise him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: These two men that you've just told us about, do you remember what they were wearing?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: They were uniforms, classic uniforms, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What language did these two men speak, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: They spoke our language.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: This interrogation that you've told us about, was that the only time you were interrogated while being detained in Livade or were you interrogated on more than one occasion?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: That was the only time we were interrogated at Livade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And when you say, sir, "we were interrogated," can you tell the Trial Chamber who you mean by "we"?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: I mean the three of us; Dr. Sikanic, Igor Guljevatej and myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You told us, sir, that you remained in this house until the morning of Sunday, 23 July 1995. At the time you left this house in Livade, were there any other prisoners detained in that house?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. During that first night of our captivity, nine more soldiers from our unit were brought in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Trivicevic, do you recall the names of these other nine soldiers from the 1st Light Infantry Brigade of Prnjavor who showed up in that house?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: I remember all their names. I can name everyone for you, if you want me to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you please do that, sir?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: Miodrag Samac, Goran Stokanovic, Vinko Aksentic, Vlado Cucic, Gojko Vujicic, Velibor Tosic, Krstan Marinkovic, Petko Maric and Dusko Pejicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: These other nine men that you've just mentioned, Mr. Trivicevic, how long did they remain in the house in Livade?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: They remained with us. When we were taken away, they were taken away too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you remember -- I'll ask you about being taken away in a moment, but do you remember anything happening shortly after this group of nine men arrived in the house? Did anything unusual happen?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: Well, perhaps I should mention the incident involving Vinko Aksentic. He was brought into a room, hands tied behind his back. They showed him a place to sit down, instead of which he leapt backwards and out through a window. The Mujahedin were petrified, unable to react for a moment. Soon they all came running outside the house. We heard sounds of shooting and we thought that they were firing at Vinko and that they had killed him. However, they soon brought him back in, and he was still conscious. Then they started beating him unconscious, and I mean that quite literally. At one point, he fainted, he started slurring. He was saying things that didn't make any sense. I can also give you an example of a young lad who was a Mujahedin. He tore Vinko's shirt off, brought it back on his leg, and had previously taken his boot off and he used his teeth to bite Vinko Aksentic's toes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Trivicevic, you mentioned a few moments ago, as reflected on line 4 of page 25: "We were taken away, they were taken away too." To where were you taken and by whom?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: By the Mujahedin. We were still prisoners of this detachment. They took us as far as a van. It was outside this van that they tore our shirts to bits and used these shreds to blindfold us so that we couldn't see where they were taking us. If I remember well, my number was number 8 in that particular line, and when it was my turn to go, there was no shred of cloth waiting for me. There was some sort of a cup made of linen that they used to pull over my head. They sat me down next to the door of the van so I could see where we were going on the way, because the cloth was transparent to some degree. I recognised on the way some buildings in Zavidovici. When they eventually stopped, it was at a place that I didn't know, that none of us recognised, but this was the Mujahedin camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you know, Mr. Trivicevic, approximately how far this location was from the town of Zavidovici?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: Well, roughly speaking, I reckon between 10 and 15 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you describe, sir, the geographic features in the immediate vicinity of this place that you have called "the Mujahedin camp"?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: This was a plateau on the side of a road, where there were two houses. At the far end of the plateau, there was a river with an enormous hill just behind it, behind which the sun takes a very long time to emerge. This is the best description I can provide. West of the road, there was the camp. South of the road, there was the river, and behind the river there was this enormous hill.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you know, Mr. Trivicevic, the name of the river that was near the camp?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, the name of the river is the Gostovic. We learned that when one of the Mujahedin threatened one of the prisoners there, saying, "Careful what you do. Otherwise, the Gostovic River might just have to carry your head away."

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you describe for the Trial Chamber what you observed in this location that you've called "the Mujahedin camp"?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: At the time that I saw this clearly, there was a house there that had burned down, and there was -- they picked another peculiar feature, what we refer to as a weeping willow in my language. There was a particular place where the Mujahedin unit would be lined up. They used this as a football pitch when they weren't, in fact, lining up. And then there was a large number of tents all around. At the entrance to the camp, there were two flags. To the left of the entrance, a black flag with a round coat of arms right in the middle and a writing in Arabic. To the right, it was a green flag or a black flag, I can't quite remember, with some Arabic lettering.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Trivicevic, I'm wondering if you can help clarify something for us. On page 26, lines 20 and 21, you say: "This was a plateau on the side of a road where there were two houses." Then on page 27, at line 9, you say: "At the time that I saw this clearly, there was a house that had burned down." Do you remember, sir, how many houses there were at this place that you have called "the Mujahedin camp"?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: Two, but at the time, the moment that I was describing, there was a tent behind which we stood, and the tent was in our line of sight, so we couldn't see the other house. So when I talked about the one house, I meant I couldn't see the other house at the time from where I was standing, so that's why.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, do you recall, sir, the approximate time and date that you arrived at this place, the Mujahedin camp?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: The 23rd of July, 1995. The time, about noon, Sunday.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber what happened upon your arrival at this location?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: They opened the van door, grabbed us by the restraints around our ankles, so they pulled us out by our feet, in a manner of speaking, our heads bumping against the ground. They were towing us, two each, along the gravel and the dust all the way up to the gate, the camp gate. We were starved and parched. It was unbearably hot in the van and outside, so we asked to have some water. The man brought a jerry can filled with water. We were lying face down on the ground, so he poured the water into the dirt and the dust, and he said, "If you can use this, all right, drink some. If not, there's nothing else I can do for you."

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And how many -- how long, sir, were you in this place that you've called "the Mujahedin camp"?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: Until the 23rd of August, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And how many people were in your group on the date that you arrived?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: When we got there, there was a group there containing the 12 men whose names I just mentioned a while ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And when you left, sir, on the 23rd of August, 1995, how many of you left?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: Eleven.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I note the time. This might be a convenient place for the break. I do have one request. This witness, on a previous occasion in giving testimony or giving a statement to local authorities, drew a very detailed sketch of this camp. I would ask, with the Trial Chamber's leave, that he be permitted to draw such a similar sketch during the break, which would save us some time, some in-court time, and then we should show that to the Defence and then question the witness about the sketch after the recess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, we can accept that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You can accept that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I would then ask if the witness could be provided with a blank piece of paper, perhaps a couple of pieces in case he needs two or three pieces. I would also indicate, with the Trial Chamber's leave, that I do expect that my direct will take a little bit longer than the one hour and 30 minutes that I'd anticipated. I do have a few more questions to put to the witness, a few documents to show him, two video clips and some still photographs. I think I can finish in perhaps 30 to 45 minutes. I think I have about 15 minutes left of my -- of my expected time, but I am asking that I be allowed to continue until the conclusion of the direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And is that a convenient time?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: It is, indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Then we will take a break and come back at 4.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Trivicevic, during the break did you have an opportunity to draw a sketch of the location that you've called "the Mujahedin camp"?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I did the best I could.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS

And I'll stop you at certain points and ask you to put identifying information on, so if you could please go very slowly.

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: In this sketch, the first thing I drew was the road [indicates]. The river is on the other side of the road. I think it is the Gostovic River. This is where the entrance to the camp was, flags on either side. Not far from there, a large tent where the Mujahedin said their prayers. This is the weeping willow [indicates]. And this is the house in which we were being held [indicates]. This is the other house right behind [indicates]. This is the Mujahedin commander's tent whom they called "Emir" [indicates]. This is the ground where they would line up and play football [indicates], and all around were the tents in which they probably slept.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, Mr. Trivicevic, the first thing that you indicated was the road. I would ask you now, with a marker, if you could please place the number "1" on what you have identified or drawn as the road.

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you. The next thing you mentioned was the river on the other side of the road. Could you please the number "2" on the sketch to denote the river.

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The next place or feature that you described was the entrance to the camp. Please place the number "3" on the entrance.

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You also mentioned flags on either side. Where were the flags, sir?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: The flags were to the left of the entrance, the black flag with a round coat of arms in the middle. To the right was the other flag. As I said, I don't exactly remember what colour it was, but it had a writing on it in Arabic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you please, sir, place the number "4" next to where you saw the black flag with a round coat of arms in the middle? Place the number "4" by where the black flag was.

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And place the number "5" near where you saw the flag with the Arabic writing on it.

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, the next thing that you mentioned, this is line 2 of page 31: "Not far from there, a large tent where the Mujahedin said their prayers." Can you please place the number "6" next to the large tent where the Mujahedin said their prayers?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Next, you described or mentioned a weeping willow. Please place the number "7" next to the weeping willow.

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I suggest that that "7" be written outside that willow, because it doesn't read like a "7" inside.

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Next, sir, you said: "This is the house in which we were being held." Please place the number "8" inside the house where you were held.

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You then said: "This is the other house right behind." Please place the number "9" in the other house.

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Next, you said, line 5, page 31: "This is the Mujahedin commander's tent whom they called 'Emir.'" Please place the number "10" on the tent you described as the Mujahedin commander's tent?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Next, Mr. Trivicevic, lines 6 and 7 of page 31, you said: "This is the ground where they would line up and play football." Please place the number "11" in the area where they would line up and play football.

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And finally, sir, you said: "All around were the tents in which they probably slept." Can you please place the number "12" next to the tents where they probably slept?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, sir, there are a number of other what appear to be the same type of figures that you've drawn as reflecting the tents below number 11 and above number 11. What, to the best of your knowledge, were those?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: Those were tents as well, it's just I couldn't get them all under the same number.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Perhaps, then, if you could place the number "12" above -- on the tents that are above number 11 so that we know that those are all the same.

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: There is a feature -- if the sketch could be centralised, please. There is a drawing to the right of number 6. What's that, a rectangular drawing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's a shack, a wooden shack made of planks. There were two or three bathrooms inside or something like that, and a toilet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we then place number "13" on that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Then to the left of the first "12" that you wrote, in very faint lines there's something that looks like a road coming to the road that is number 1. What is that, the faint line --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a small creek [marks], a rather small creek. This is the confluence between the creek and the Gostovic River. I think there was a small bridge here [indicates] with some pipes, insulated pipes, which we assumed were used to heat water inside the camp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we put number "14" next to the creek.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Then on the area marked as number 11, there's that jagged line. I don't know whether it was used just to say -- to denote the entire area or whether it means anything.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I just drew this to mark off the area of the level ground. The tents all around were slightly elevated in relation to this central portion, so that's all I used it for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. We'll hold on to this map or this sketch. I might have the witness mark one or two other places as the testimony progresses, and then of course we'll tender this into evidence. Before we do that, I would ask that a clip be shown from P06032. This is approximately four minutes' long. We will play it without the audio, and I'll ask the witness some questions about what he observes on the tape once we've had a chance to look at this tape. It's approximately four minutes' long.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And are we going to hear the audio at some stage?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's -- again, it's a tape that basically consists of narration. I'm not in a position to indicate who made the narration or when the narration was made, so we probably will not be playing the audio, unless, of course, we have subsequent witnesses who have relevant information concerning it. We're simply showing the images so that the witness, if he's in a position to tell us what the video depicts, can do so, and then we'll show him some stills from that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, you may or may not be aware, but today the Defence filed a response in respect of the audio clip that the Prosecution had previously filed a motion in respect of, and in that response we have strongly suggested that video evidence should not be altered, so that we should see both images and sound together. And I adopt the same position in respect of this clip now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I had anticipated that objection. That's why I asked the question, "Are we going to hear the audio at some stage," because you have made this objection before.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Yes. We're being consistent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's right, and I was trying to anticipate it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: We're fine. If the Defence wants the audio played, we'll play the audio as well. I will --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It goes with that argument of no changes or deletions to an exhibit, let's get the entire exhibit as it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: That's fine. And I take it, then, from the Defence position, as reflected on what my learned colleague said, that there will be no more objections to any video that has labelling on it, because of course that goes to the same issue in terms of whether evidence is -- material on evidence is redacted or otherwise altered. There might be some of the photos today that we're showing that have redactions that were previously done because of Defence concerns that were raised earlier, but henceforward we will no longer make such redactions to either the videotapes or to the stills derived therefrom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: We'll go ahead and play this audio clip. I do apologise to the language booths. I don't believe that they have the transcripts. It's a relatively short clip, and there is likely to be some language spoken that is not in B/C/S, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And there are no subtitles?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: There are no subtitles on this tape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Trivicevic, can you please comment on the videotape that we've all just seen, in terms of what was depicted on that tape?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: The footage shows the camp where we spent a month in captivity. What is shown here are most of the things that I mentioned in my sketch, in my diagram, and that I marked with numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I would ask, first of all, that that video clip be admitted into evidence, and second of all, I do have a number of still photographs taken from this video, and I would ask that those be shown to the witness and that he be allowed to explain to us what's on the still photos.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness has stated that the video clip shows the camp as which they were held, so I would concede there is a basis upon which this document could be admitted into evidence. However, I would like to state for the record that just because the video clip had the heading "El Mujahedin" on it doesn't mean that we, as Defence, concede that this document was prepared by the El Mujahedin Detachment. We reserve the right to challenge the authenticity or we would expect the Prosecution to call further evidence to establish the authenticity of this document in due course. But we don't oppose its admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The video clip is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will become Exhibit 546, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Trivicevic, a number of photographs, still photographs taken from this video clip that we've just observed, have been placed on the machine to your right. I'm wondering, sir, if you can explain to us what's visible in this first photograph that's actually on the machine to your right or visible on the screen in front of you. Can you describe for us what you see in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: The shot was taken from the place where we were, the playground and the review area, and you can clearly see the weeping willow, you can see the house where we were held, and you can see the other house behind. You can see the flag that was at the entrance to the camp, to the right side.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, perhaps for ease -- to make this as simple as possible, if the sketch that the witness drew could be placed in front of him or perhaps on the ELMO as well. If they could both -- I want to show him both so that he can put the same numbers on the photograph that he marked on the sketch. I think that might be the best way to do this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, sir, you mentioned that you could see in the photograph the weeping willow. On the sketch, you've marked the weeping willow, I believe, with the number "7". Could you place the number "7" on this photograph to reflect the weeping willow?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And the house that you were kept in, what number is that on the sketch?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: Number 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You've marked that on the photograph. And the other house, sir?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]. The other house is number 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can you please look at the next photograph. Can you tell us what's visible in this photograph, sir?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: It's a shot taken in the same place and then of the markers mentioned, all you can see is the weeping willow and the house marked with the number "8".

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And again, sir, if you could please mark the same numbers on the photograph as you've marked on the sketch so that the numbers are consistent.

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could please then go to the next photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you describe for us what's visible in this photograph, sir?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: You can see the field where the reviews were held. You can see the playground. You can even see the goal posts here [indicates]. And then behind, to the back, you can see the tents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let's start, sir, with the tents. Can you please place the number "12" on the tents that you see in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: All the tents together are marked by number 12 [marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And the area that you've described as the field or the playground, could you place the number "11" on that area of the photograph?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]. Number 11 is here, indicating this whole area where the soldiers are, as well as the clear parts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And you also, sir, mentioned the goal posts. Could you please place an "X" on the goal post or goal posts?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And what was that goal post made of?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: Just plain wood.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we please go to the next photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you describe what is visible in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: The photograph again shows the two houses marked with numbers 8 and 9, and you can see a member of the El Mudjahedin Detachment who the Mujahedin described to us as a 12-year-old boy who had come from Saudi Arabia to fight. He personally cut my ears with a pocket knife at the house in Livade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, can you please mark -- you started out by saying that the photo shows the houses marked with the numbers "8" and "9". Can you please write the numbers "8" and "9" on the appropriate houses in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you please circle the person that you told us was described to you as a 12-year-old boy, the person who cut your ears with a pocket knife, circle that person?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please go to the next photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What's depicted, sir, in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: Again on the photograph you can see a number of tents and you can see the field where the reviews were held and where they played soccer in their free time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Again, Mr. Trivicevic, I would ask you to place the number "12" on the tents.

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The number "11" on the field.

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And "Xs" on what you have described as the goal posts.

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And finally if we could go to the last photograph in this bundle, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recognise anyone in this photograph or anything in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: The photograph shows a man who was introduced as "Abu Hamza," and you can see the flag that was to the right side of the camp entrance.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you please, sir, write the name "Abu Hamza" on the person who you have told us was introduced as "Abu Hamza?"

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Your Honours, we'd ask that this bundle of photographs be admitted into evidence and it be given a single exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The bundle of photographs is admitted into evidence. May it please be given a single exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be Exhibit 547, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Trivicevic, immediately before the break you told us, and this is reflected on line -- page 28, line 23, through page 29, line 5, that you were in this Mujahedin camp until the 23rd of August, 1995, and that there were 11 of you who left on that day. Can you tell us, sir, what happened to the 12th person who'd entered the camp with you on the 23rd of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: On the night of the 23rd and the 24th of July, 1995, we were taken out of the house where we were. Emir and a number of other Mujahedins were at the door, and they asked our prisoners who was the man who had tried to escape. But we didn't know what they were talking about at that point, and they took us one by one, with blindfolds on, to someplace in the camp where we were tied up with our legs raised so that we were in a sort of semi-hanging position. We stayed there all -- until morning, and then in the morning this 12th person, Gojko Vujicic, was killed in front of my eyes, and his head was cut off.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me -- I hate to do this, sir, but let me interrupt you at this point. Can you again return to the sketch that remains on the machine to your right? Can you indicate, if you recall, the location where you were taken on the sketch or in the camp and this location where you've told us Gojko Vujicic was killed in front of your eyes?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: According to my estimate, this was near the big tent where the prayers were held. It was a little bit above the room where the shower and the toilet were. It was not a room, it was just an area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. So this is not a building; is that what you're saying? It's simply --

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: That's right, it's not a building.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you please place the number "15" at this location where Gojko Vujicic was killed in front of your eyes?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you describe the terrain at that location that you've just marked as number 15?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: It was just an area with soil, without grass. It was dust and pebbles or stones mixed together.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you describe, sir, to the best of your recollection, what happened on that night, 23-24 July 1995, when Gojko Vujicic was killed?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: I was brought to that place, when they then raised my legs to the back. Our faces were facing the ground. It was very difficult to breathe. At one point, the Mujahedin that I knew called "Habib," who was in that group that had captured me, ran up to help me. He brought a piece of cardboard and placed it under my face so that I could breathe. He brought me a cup of coffee so that I could drink. And at one point, he untied my hands as if to help me. I couldn't move my arms or hands anywhere. They just simply dropped alongside my body. They were so numb, my arms, that I couldn't control them. And then after a while, I fell asleep. I remember very well that in my dream, when I could sense that I could control my arms again, I ripped away the tape that was blindfolding me and that was all around my head. Habib at that point approached me and took a single layer of gauze and tied that over my eyes so that I would look like all the other prisoners, so I could actually see through that layer of gauze everything that was going on. He tied my hands to my back and let my legs down, and he warned me not to even think of trying to get away. I fell asleep, and I slept all the way until morning, until the Mujahedin prayers began. This woke me up, and at that point I looked to my left side and I saw Gojko Vujicic, who I don't know how, managed to turn on his back during the night. Since he was wounded in the groin area and was suffering a lot of pain, he begged to be given some water, to be helped, or to have his arms or legs untied because he really couldn't stand it anymore, everything that was happening. The Mujahedin strictly had warned us that there could be no swearing in their presence. He started to swear, and amongst other things, he mentioned God in those curses. And one of the Mujahedin who were in the tent at prayer came out of the tent, took an automatic rifle that was right next to the entrance, and he cocked it on his way. And then walking, he stopped next to Gojko's head, and Gojko could see him coming up, and he just turned his head towards me, to his left. And then going along, he stood next to Gojko's head and coolly fired a shot to Gojko's right temple and then went back to the tent. And then I just looked at Gojko and I could see his little finger still twitching as if he were alive. The Mujahedin went to the tent, and then he took a sword, came back to Gojko, and in several strokes he severed Gojko's head. He tried to place this head on the chest, but since the body was tilting backwards, the head wouldn't stay there. He tried it several times, and when that didn't work, he placed the head on the stomach. Then it rolled off again. He put it back on the stomach, and then it stayed there. He approached me. He raised me and turned me, and he was showing me Gojko's head that was resting on Gojko's stomach and that was facing me at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Trivicevic, how long did you and the other ten men who were still alive remain at this place that you've marked as number 15 on the sketch after Gojko Vujicic was killed?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: I was there. I was the one that they untied first, and immediately after that they took me into the house where we had been captured, and then one by one, immediately one after another, they took all the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And again, sir, if need be, relying on the sketch to your right, when you say: "They took me into the house where we had been captured," can you tell us which number on your sketch you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: I'm thinking of the house marked with the number "8".

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us what happened after all the members of your group were returned to that house?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC
utterances.text: When everybody was brought back to the house, one of the Mujahedin, I don't recall which one, brought Gojko's head, hanging on a butcher's hook in the shape of a letter S, and as he was coming in from the door, he threw the head. I don't remember the order. He either threw it to Krstan Marinkovic or Igor Guljevatej. One of them held the head on their lap. And then there were all sorts of excesses going on, and then they took the head from one detainee to another, saying, "Kiss your brother."
